content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"The Ancient of Days is a symbolic title for the eternal God (most commonly God the Father) enthroned as sovereign heavenly Judge in Daniel 7; His agedness signifies eternal pre-existence, wisdom, and supreme judicial authority, with the main live dispute being whether the figure is the Father, Christ, or God without personal specification.","book_summary":"The Ancient of Days is the venerable One at the origin and advancement of days—still the divine figure of Daniel 7, but portrayed as seated at the head of a calendar cycle, the day from which the month, year, and age advance, adding a 'calendar office' the common teaching (eternity/pre-existence only) does not include.","consensus_core_identification":"A divine title for the eternal God enthroned as Judge; 'ancient' = eternal pre-existence and sovereign authority.","book_core_identification":"The divine One 'advanced in days' who presides at the head of the cycle of days—God holding a calendar office as origin and advancer of days, months, years, and ages.","core_relation":"BOOK_BROADENS","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"Both readings identify the same referent (God in Daniel 7:9, 13, 22), but the book reinterprets the sense of 'ancient of days': instead of a metaphor solely for eternity/pre-existence and judgeship, it assigns the figure an additional functional role as head of the calendar cycle from which days and ages advance. The book explicitly flags that the common view teaches 'no calendar office,' so the disagreement is over what the title predicates of God, not over who the figure is or which passages it covers.","material_contradiction":"None at the level of referent. The book does not deny divinity, enthronement, or judgment; it adds a calendrical function the consensus does not recognize. The claims are compatible unless the book elsewhere denies eternity/pre-existence, which this entry does not do.","rationale":"Reduced to cores: consensus says the Ancient of Days = the eternal God enthroned as Judge; the book says the Ancient of Days = the venerable divine One at the origin and advancement of days, seated at the head of the calendar cycle. The central referent (the enthroned God of Daniel 7) is preserved, and the covered occurrences are identical (Dan 7:9, 13, 22 only, which both sides note). The material change is a precision/boundary shift in the meaning of the title—adding a calendar office and reframing 'ancient of days' as positional (head of the advancing cycle of days) rather than purely qualitative (eternally pre-existent). Since this preserves the consensus category (a divine title of the enthroned God) while materially altering what the title asserts, REFINED with BOOK_BROADENS fits better than DIVERGENT (no replaced referent) or NOVEL (the divine-title identification is squarely within consensus).","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue for MATCH: the 'calendar office' language may be mere rhetorical repackaging of the same idea of God's eternity and primacy over time (Ps 93:2 'from everlasting,' Isa 43:13 'before the day was I am he'), in which case the book's core is equivalent to the consensus and the difference is only wording. However, the book's own common-view note explicitly marks 'no calendar office' as the point of departure, signaling the author intends a real interpretive addition, not a paraphrase.","confidence":"medium"}
